title: FC Barcelona ‘La Masia’ academy: a global brand that drives the club’s identity and sporting excellence
abstract: The primary goal of this research is to examine the crucial role of FC Barcelona’s La Masia academy in developing elite players for the club. It explores how La Masia has contributed to shaping FC Barcelona’s identity, particularly its distinctive style of play. The study combines quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Quantitatively, it analyses data from 1980 to 2024, including first-team squad composition, trophy outcomes, and player market values, using descriptive statistics and comparative analysis. Qualitatively, it draws on in-depth interviews with key figures linked to La Masia’s history, as well as a former professional footballer offering an external perspective. These interviews address the academy’s evolution, development processes, and influence on the club’s identity and success. Findings highlight La Masia’s importance in sustaining sporting performance and institutional identity, while showing its impact is shaped by managerial decisions and external recruitment strategies, contributing to broader discussions on talent development and sport management.

title: MODERN METHODS FOR IMPROVING STROKE TECHNIQUE IN TABLE TENNIS PLAYERS
venue: JOURNAL OF EDUCATION, ETHICS AND VALUE
abstract: Table tennis is a highly dynamic sport that requires athletes to demonstrate exceptional technical precision, coordination, reaction speed, physical fitness, and tactical awareness. The effectiveness of competitive performance largely depends on the quality of stroke execution, the ability to control the racket, the regulation of ball speed and rotation, and the selection of appropriate technical actions under constantly changing playing conditions. In contemporary table tennis, the increasing speed of competitive play and the development of advanced playing techniques require the continuous improvement of traditional training methods and the implementation of scientifically grounded pedagogical approaches. The development of stroke technique should therefore be considered a comprehensive process involving biomechanical efficiency, motor learning, physical preparation, technical repetition, visual perception, and individual adaptation. This article examines modern methods for improving stroke technique in table tennis players, focusing on the theoretical, methodological, and practical foundations of technical preparation. Particular attention is given to forehand and backhand strokes, topspin, backspin, blocking, counterattacking, serving, and receiving techniques. The article analyzes the importance of biomechanical principles, coordinated body movement, racket control, correct timing, movement accuracy, and the effective transfer of body-generated force into ball movement. Modern pedagogical approaches, including multiball training, variable practice, individualized instruction, video feedback, target-based exercises, game-based learning, and digital performance analysis, are discussed as important instruments for improving technical mastery. title: Cooperación mediante juegos tradicionales en Educación Física de la Educación Básica ecuatoriana
abstract: La enseñanza de la cooperación mediante juegos tradicionales exige distinguir la participación grupal de un aprendizaje social intencional. Este artículo analiza las posibilidades, condiciones y límites de estas prácticas para la Educación Física de la Educación Básica ecuatoriana. Se desarrolló una revisión narrativa crítica de publicaciones académicas recientes, complementada con documentación curricular oficial. La búsqueda se realizó mediante buscadores académicos y portales editoriales, con términos en español e inglés sobre juegos tradicionales, aprendizaje cooperativo, educación física, inclusión y relaciones sociales. Se diferenciaron investigaciones escolares, estudios universitarios, revisiones y aportes conceptuales; además, se explicitó cuándo el acceso se limitó al resumen. La síntesis muestra que las intervenciones cooperativas presentan resultados favorables en distintos dominios educativos, aunque existe heterogeneidad y no puede atribuirse el mismo efecto a cualquier juego tradicional. Los estudios sobre emociones, habilidades motrices y percepciones aportan información complementaria, pero no demuestran por sí solos cambios duraderos en cooperación. La evidencia ecuatoriana examinada ofrece pertinencia cultural y experiencias inclusivas, con restricciones para establecer causalidad o generalizar entre subniveles. Se propone una matriz de coherencia entre reglas, interdependencia, participación equitativa, mediación docente y evaluación observable, acompañada de orientaciones diferenciadas para Preparatoria, Elemental, Media y Superior. Esta contribución constituye una propuesta didáctica pendiente de validación local. title: Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport
venue: Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
abstract: Egon Brunswik proposed the concept of "representative design" for psychological experimentation, which has historically been overlooked or confused with another of Brunswik's terms, ecological validity. In this article, we reiterate the distinction between these two important concepts and highlight the relevance of the term representative design for sports psychology, practice, and experimental design. We draw links with ideas on learning design in the constraints-led approach to motor learning and nonlinear pedagogy. We propose the adoption of a new term, representative learning design, to help sport scientists, experimental psychologists, and pedagogues recognize the potential application of Brunswik's original concepts, and to ensure functionality and action fidelity in training and learning environments.

title: Ecological approaches to cognition and action in sport and exercise: Ask not only what you do, but where you do it
abstract: In recent decades, concepts and ideas from James J. Gibson's theory of direct perception in ecological psychology have been applied to the study of how perception and action regulate sport performance. This article examines the influence of different streams of thought in ecological psychology for studying cognition and action in the diverse behavioural contexts of sport and exercise. In discussing the origins of ecological psychology it can be concluded that psychologists such as Lewin, and to some extent Heider, provided the initial impetus for the development of key ideas. We argue that the papers in this special issue clarify that the different schools of thinking in ecological psychology have much to contribute to theoretical and practical developments in sport and exercise psychology. For example, Gibson emphasized and formalized how the individual is coupled with the environment; Brunswik raised the issue of the ontology of probability in human behaviour and the problem of representative design for experimental task constraints; Barker looked carefully into extra-individual behavioural contexts and Bronfenbrenner presented insights pertinent to the relations between behaviour contexts, and macro influences on behaviour. In this overview, we highlight essential issues from the main schools of thought of relevance to the contexts of sport and exercise, and we consider some potential theoretical linkages with dynamical systems theory.

title: The dynamics of expertise acquisition in sport: The role of affective learning design
How Elite Coaches' Experiential Knowledge Might Enhance Empirical Research on Sport Performance
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: In sport science, much research has been aimed at developing empirical knowledge of performance and practice. While this body of work has led to significant advances in understanding, one source of information that has been under-represented is the analysis of experiential knowledge of highlevel athletes and coaches. Using the run-up task in sport as an exemplar, we were interested in understanding the relationship between the experiential knowledge of elite coaches and empirical research findings to ascertain how a combination of these knowledge sources might enrich understanding of sport performance. For this purpose, fifteen interviews were conducted with elite coaches from three sports; track and field, gymnastics, and cricket. The qualitative data showed elite coaches intuitively expressed ideas consistent with recent scientific research in their design of training and learning programs. Key ideas expressed included perception-action coupling, the effects of interacting constraints on performance, and an approach to practice which was consistent with insights from nonlinear pedagogy. The data revealed how experiential knowledge of elite coaches might be used to support and enhance empirical research processes. Specific examples include providing direction for future research, assisting in the representative design of empirical research, and highlighting limitations of some empirical research protocols and findings. The coaches' comments suggested a need for more systematic and sustained efforts to explore how experiential knowledge might enrich understanding of sport performance.

title: Representative design: Does the addition of a defender change the execution of a basketball shot?

The role of representative design in talent development: a comment on “Talent identification and promotion programmes of Olympic athletes”
abstract:
A recent comment in the Journal of Sports Sciences (MacNamara & Collins, 2011) highlighted some major concerns with the current structure of talent identification and development (TID) programmes of Olympic athletes (e.g. Gulbin, 2008; Vaeyens, Gullich, Warr, & Philippaerts, 2009). In a cogent commentary, MacNamara and Collins (2011) provided a short review of the extant literature, which was both timely and insightful. Specifically, they criticised the ubiquitous one-dimensional ‘physically-biased’ attempts to produce world class performers, emphasising the need to consider a number of key environmental variables in a more multi-disciplinary perspective. They also lamented the wastage of talent, and alluded to the operational and opportunistic nature of current talent transfer programmes. A particularly compelling aspect of the comment was their allusion to high profile athletes who had ‘failed’ performance evaluation tests and then proceeded to succeed in that sport. This issue identifies a problem with current protocols for evaluating performance and is a line of research that is sorely needed in the area of talent development. To understand the nature of talent wastage that might be occurring in high performance programmes in sport, future empirical work should seek to follow the career paths of ‘successful’ and ‘unsuccessful’ products of TID programmes, in comparative analyses. Pertinent to the insights of MacNamara and Collins (2011), it remains clear that a number of questions have not received enough attention from sport scientists interested in talent development, including:

title: Measuring Skill in Rugby Union and Rugby League as Part of the Standard Team Testing Battery
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Coaches, strength and conditioning coaches, and researchers typically use a standard testing battery as a screening tool to measure physical characteristics of players. The information from this testing battery is subsequently utilized to check whether a player can meet the demands of the sport, talent identification, long-term player development, squad/team selection and/or for designing training programs. Apart from these physical attributes, Rugby players (both Union and League) also need to efficiently execute a range of technical and tactical skills during a match. Attempts to assess skill in Rugby have been reported, but little has been documented on assessing skill as part of a Rugby team testing battery. This review highlights the use of, and requirements of, a skill assessment that can be used in a Rugby team setting. When devising a skill assessment, a number of factors such as standardisation, validity, reliability, logistics, player safety, ecological validity, and representative design need to be considered. All these factors should be considered on a continuum, and not in absolute terms. The 1 vs 1 attacker and defender interactions allow for an acceptable degree of ecological validity and representative design, and logistically seems most appealing for team testing. Also, using a valid and reliable set of technical criteria and outcome measures has shown to be most appropriate to standardise a skill assessment.

title: Achieving external validity in home advantage research: generalizing crowd noise effects
abstract: Different factors have been postulated to explain the home advantage phenomenon in sport. One plausible explanation investigated has been the influence of a partisan home crowd on sports officials' decisions. Different types of studies have tested the crowd influence hypothesis including purposefully designed experiments. However, while experimental studies investigating crowd influences have high levels of internal validity, they suffer from a lack of external validity; decision-making in a laboratory setting bearing little resemblance to decision-making in live sports settings. This focused review initially considers threats to external validity in applied and theoretical experimental research. Discussing how such threats can be addressed using representative design by focusing on a recently published study that arguably provides the first experimental evidence of the impact of live crowd noise on officials in sport. The findings of this controlled experiment conducted in a real tournament setting offer a level of confirmation of the findings of laboratory studies in the area. Finally directions for future research and the future conduct of crowd noise studies are discussed.

title: Skill acquisition and representative task design
abstract: Egon Brunswik's (1956) insights have revealed that representative task design is a key concept in understanding the organization of task constraints in experiments, evaluation tests and learning programmes in sport. Representative design implies that these environments need to be predicated on key information sources found in specific performance contexts. Although Brunswik's ideas have, until now, failed to be fully appreciated in a wide range of experimental and behavioural sciences, many of the concepts have begun to be accepted in the study of complex systems in sport (Araújo and Davids 2009; Beek et al. 2003; Davids 2008; Dicks et al. 2008; Fajen et al. 2009; Pinder et al. 2011b,c). Here, we discuss the ideas of representative task design and examine its implications for constructing experimental and learning environments in sport. We provide principles for sport scientists, experimental psychologists and pedagogues to recognize the potential application and adaptation of Brunswik's original concepts, with examples from various sports to demonstrate how the model can be applied in practice. We also discuss the role of representative design in supporting the psychology of learning and creating holistic learning environments for learners as complex systems, in addition to considering the integrated emotional engagement of participants for the enhancement of learning and practice task design.

title: Informational constraints on performance of dynamic interceptive actions
abstract: Utilising quantitative and qualitative research methods the thesis explored how movement patterns were coordinated under different conditions in elite athletes. Results revealed each elite athlete's ability to use multiple, varied information sources to guide successful task performance, highlighting the specific role of surrounding objects in the performance environment to perceptually guide behaviour. Combining elite coaching knowledge with empirical research enhanced understanding of the role of vision in regulating interceptive behaviours, enhancing the representative design of training environments. The main findings have been applied to training design of the Athletics Australia National Jumps Centre at the Queensland Academy of Sport in preparation for the World Indoor Championships, World Championships, and Olympic Games for Australian long and triple jumpers.

title: Training Adaptable Astronauts: Integrating Ecological Psychology into Human Performance in Space Missions
abstract: Astronauts must acquire, adapt, and maintain complex perceptual–motor skills while operating in environments that are novel, variable, and challenging. With human spaceflight shifting from low-Earth orbit missions to long-duration expeditions on the Moon and Mars, these demands intensify as astronauts face altered gravitational fields, along with other challenges like communication delays and high-stakes technical tasks. Despite decades of advances in engineering and physiology, astronaut training has only minimally integrated evidence-based principles from ecological psychology, that views skill learning as the ongoing attunement to affordances, which are action possibilities that emerge from the interaction between the individual and the environment. This paper examines how ecological frameworks, such as ecological dynamics, the constraints-led approach, perception–action coupling, affordance theory, and representative design, could refresh the design of astronaut training. Drawing on examples also from elite sport, ecologically grounded methods such as representative simulations, variable constraint manipulation, and affordance-rich training environments, are proposed to enhance adaptability, skill retention, and autonomy in long-duration missions. These approaches aim to ensure that astronauts remain perceptually attuned and operationally resilient in the unpredictable conditions of deep-space exploration.

title: Using virtual environments to study interactions in sport performance
abstract: This chapter highlights the potential of immersive, interactive virtual reality technology to study dynamical interactions in sport performance. In view of the continuous advances in this technology, the dilemma between maintaining task representative design and guaranteeing experimental control has ceased to exist. The advantages and disadvantages of this methodological tool for the design of both practice and research-based experimental tasks that intend to improve and investigate the dynamics of environment-agent systems and information-action coupling in sports, are reviewed and discussed. Virtual reality technology is highlighted, as it allows us to capture the complexity of actions yet to control the presentation of information (mainly visual and auditory but also haptic/tactile) that guides action.

title: An examination of learning design in elite springboard diving
abstract: The overarching aim of this programme of work was to evaluate the effectiveness of the existing learning environment within the Australian Institute of Sport (AIS) elite springboard diving programme. Unique to the current research programme, is the application of ideas from an established theory of motor learning, specifically ecological dynamics, to an applied high performance training environment. In this research programme springboard diving is examined as a complex system, where individual, task, and environmental constraints are continually interacting to shape performance. As a consequence, this thesis presents some necessary and unique insights into representative learning design and movement adaptations in a sample of elite athletes. The questions examined in this programme of work relate to how best to structure practice, which is central to developing an effective learning environment in a high performance setting. Specifically, the series of studies reported in the chapters of this doctoral thesis: (i) provide evidence for the importance of designing representative practice tasks in training; (ii) establish that completed and baulked (prematurely terminated) take-offs are not different enough to justify the abortion of a planned dive; and (iii), confirm that elite athletes performing complex skills are able to adapt their movement patterns to achieve consistent performance outcomes from variable dive take-off conditions. Chapters One and Two of the thesis provide an overview of the theoretical ideas framing the programme of work, and include a review of literature pertinent to the research aims and subsequent empirical chapters. title: Promoting perception–action coupling in sport: the role of preparation within coaching environments
abstract: In recent years, there has been considerable interest in the coupling of perception and action and resultant practices for supporting the exploration of perceptual motor landscapes (e.g. through representative design). Although perception–action coupling can capably explain the organisation of behaviour and action in some contexts, there are also some noteworthy issues and challenges with its scholarship and application (e.g. within coaching or team-sport environments). With this in mind, this paper initially reviews current evidence and associated issues with perception–action coupling and its mechanisms. From here, we offer proposals for addressing identified limitations. In particular, we contend that a priori planning and preparation are key to optimising the efficacy and operation of perception–action coupling within performance settings. As part of this, we explore whether movement control may be better explained by alternative approaches (e.g. predictive processing) and more effectively facilitated through a wider set of coaching andpsychology tools.

title: The environment design principles
abstract: The environment design principles (EDP) operationalise the constraints-led approach by providing user-friendly principles to support coaches in the practice environment design process. The EDP consist of four principles that capture the core theoretical foundations of ecological dynamics. Principle 1 emphasises the role and importance of session intention in the environment design process. Principle 2 brings together the concepts of constraints and affordances, challenging coaches to manipulate constraints to systematically design-in affordances to the practice environment. Principle 3 requires coaches to consider the impact that representative design has on learning transfer. Principle 4 considers the concept of practice variability and requires coaches to manage how much variability they should design-in to the practice environment. Each principle has its own unique purpose, resultantly impacting upon decisions a coach will make in the environment design process. A key feature common across sport is the belief of practitioners that we become ‘skilled’ by doing repetition after repetition.

title: Representing reality: Investigating the perception-action couplings of expert soccer Goalkeepers under representative constraints
abstract: Representative Design has become a frequently used term across sport science (Pinder et al. 2011). Brunswiks original assertion that there “is little technical basis for telling whether a given experiment is an ecological normal, located in the midst of a crowd of natural instances, or whether it is more like a bearded lady at the fringes of reality” (Brunswik, 1955, p.204) led towards a key concept, representation design. Brunswik (1955, p.198) proposed that researchers “must resist the temptation {. . .} to interfere” with the environment and “instead strive to retain its natural causal texture in the stimuli presented to participants” (Dhami et al, 2004 p.962). In football goalkeeping, early work on expertise used a penalty kick task in in-situ and digital environments (See Savelsbergh et al. 2002). Whilst the findings are interesting, it is worth proceeding with caution and attention should be turned towards creating representative experiments that are reflective of the environment the individual inhabits. This study attempted to show differences in perceptual behaviours between a traditional task, and a representative task. In a professional football case study, 4 goalkeepers took part in both conditions over a season. Using the Quiet Eye(QE) (Vickers, 1996) as the perceptual mechanism for analysis, eye behaviours were recorded via an SMI-ETG mobile device, and coded with a Vision-In-Action system. QE duration was significantly longer (t2=2.66,P≤0.05) in Penalty trial (PT) than in the Representative trial (RT) (50.75%±2.84% v 45.57%±0.93%). QE onset occurred significantly (t2=4.75,P<0.05) earlier in PT than in RT (21.13%±4.21% v 36.38%±4.30%). title: Turning up the variable noise: the quiet eye, functional variability and advancements in perceptual cognitive expertise
abstract: Background: It has now become widely accepted that a prominent component of sport expertise is in part due to more effective, and efficient perceptual mechanisms. In comparison to lesser-skilled athletes, experts can identify key sources of information earlier (Helsen and Pauwels, 1993). With the introduction of the Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules within the English Football League System, the development of young players has increased in prominence, with a greater emphasis on the understanding of what it takes to become an expert. The Quiet Eye (QE) has emerged as a key perceptual variable associated with expertise (Vickers, 2007). The QE is defined as the final fixation towards a location in the environment that supports a coupled motor action. The QE is a fixation that lasts over 100ms, remaining within 3* of visual angle (Vickers, 2016). In the field of Goalkeeping (GK) the QE has been found to be one of the key mechanisms in understanding skilled performance (Piras and Vickers, 2011). It is widely accepted that expert performance is generally contrived of longer QE fixations, earlier and later offsets, yet the locations GK’s use is still contested. As such current experimental protocols fail to truly understand expert performance of individuals in more complex environments. Objectives: Theoretical and empirical attempts are made to meet an ecological ‘call to arms’ and challenge the traditional perceptual research in goalkeeping. The importance of maintaining a representative experimental trial is stressed to understand expertise from the natural performance environment. title: Game statistic-based performance indicators in wheelchair basketball: A systematic review of trends and insights
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Wheelchair basketball (WB) performance analysis has expanded, yet evidence remains dispersed across box-score, observational and model-based approaches, and no synthesis has integrated the indicators, data sources and analytical methods used across player, team and line-up levels. This systematic review examined how game-related statistics (GRS) have been used to analyse WB performance and identified performance indicators, data sources and analytical methods applied in competition. Searches were conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus and EBSCO-SPORTDiscus, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation tracking. Following PRISMA 2020, studies were eligible if they analysed quantitative match statistics from official WB competitions. Data extraction covered competition context, dataset type, GRS, analytical approach and key findings, and methodological quality was assessed using a 16-item checklist adapted from the Critical Review Form for Quantitative Studies. Eighteen studies were included: 11 used box-score or match-statistics datasets, and 7 used observational sequence-, possession-, shot-, or screen-based datasets. Shooting efficiency, assist- and turnover-related indicators, and rebounding were most consistently associated with success. Functional classification shaped statistical output, although clustering and optimisation studies showed that performance profiles were not determined by classification alone. Most studies relied on descriptive or inferential comparisons, while fewer applied predictive modelling, clustering or Bayesian optimisation. Common limitations included inconsistent standardisation, limited possession-level adjustment and incomplete modelling of contextual and hierarchical structures. title: From rigid marks to robust perception: Practice variability fosters flexible time-to-contact timing in a virtual reality relay simulator
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: The 4×100-meter relay presents a fundamental motor paradox: maximizing running speed while ensuring millisecond-precision baton transmission. Traditionally, receivers start when their partner reaches a fixed ground mark, a time-to-passage (TTP) strategy that makes them vulnerable to fluctuations in the partner's approach speed. This study evaluated an immersive virtual reality (VR) relay simulator in which receivers learned to initiate their run at a critical time-to-contact (TTC) with the incoming partner, without any ground mark. Twenty-two novice participants practiced with self-controlled feedback, either at a constant approach speed (stable group) or at three approach speeds varying from trial to trial (variable group). All completed a pre-test, acquisition, a post-test, a five-day retention test and a transfer test at a novel approach speed. Absolute timing error decreased significantly between pre-test and retention in both groups, validating task learning. At transfer, however, accuracy declined markedly in the stable group, whereas the variable group maintained its previously acquired accuracy. The constant error of the stable group (+162 ms) closely matched the value predicted if run initiation relied on an optical correlate of distance (+160 ms), while the near-zero constant error of the variable group (+13 ms) indicated reliance on information about TTC. Practice variability thus breaks the confound between TTC and lower-order optical variables, promoting the use of more robust optical information and behavioral flexibility. Shifting from TTP to TTC-based training in VR offers a promising alternative to rigid ground marks for relay training.

Dose–response relationship between weekly physical activity volume and depressive symptoms among Chinese adults: a cross-sectional analysis of a national sports and society survey
abstract: Background Identifying modifiable protective factors for depression remains a public health priority. This cross-sectional study examined the shape of the dose–response relationship between weekly physical activity (PA) volume and depressive symptoms among Chinese adults. Methods This cross-sectional analysis used the 2024 National Sports and Society Survey and included 11,379 adults with complete data on PA volume and depressive symptoms (complete-case sample, n = 10,096). PA volume was measured with an IPAQ-type instrument and expressed as MET-min/week; depressive symptoms with the CES-D-10 (score ≥ 10). Logistic regression used stepwise adjustment, with restricted cubic splines and survey-weighted sensitivity analyses. Results The weighted prevalence of depressive symptoms was 25.2%. Restricted cubic splines showed a broadly inverse, non-linear association ( p = 0.001), with the lowest odds near 4,000 MET-min/week. Each 1-SD increase in log-transformed PA volume was associated with an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 0.87 (95% CI 0.83–0.91), and the highest quartile had 29% lower odds than the lowest (aOR 0.71, 95% CI 0.63–0.80). The association was directionally consistent across subgroups, but attenuated toward the null under the raw survey weights and sensitive to weight trimming. Conclusion Higher weekly PA volume was associated with lower odds of depressive symptoms in a non-linear, broadly inverse pattern. The association was sensitive to survey weighting, and the cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation.

title: Measuring the perceptions of transfer of sports-based skills to the job market and their policy implications
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Introduction Academic research has found that participation in sport can have physiological, psychological, and social benefits. The objective of this paper is to investigate the socio-professional advantages that can be gained through participation in competitive sport and the policies that could be resulting from them. Methods This research was based on a questionnaire distributed to 659 individuals from 56 countries with the aim of identifying whether they perceived that their participation in competitive sport has instilled in them job transferable soft skills such as leadership, time management, teamwork, decision-making, and ability to work under pressure. Results The results showed that most of the participants have highlighted that sport has provided them several soft skills that were very beneficial in their professional career. Discussion These positive outcomes can lead to the elaboration of policies that can raise the awareness on the societal benefits of competitive sport, develop the subject of physical education and sports in schools and universities curricula and strengthen a country's national power.

title: Regenerative braking strategy for mine electric rubber-tired vehicles based on fuzzy control optimized by an improved whale optimization algorithm
abstract: Mine electric rubber-tired vehicles in confined underground environments suffer from limited driving range and inefficient braking energy recovery. Existing fuzzy regenerative braking strategies rely on empirical tuning and struggle to satisfy both braking safety and energy economy. This paper proposes a regenerative braking fuzzy control strategy optimized by an improved whale optimization algorithm under Economic Commission for Europe braking regulations. A front- and rear-axle braking force distribution strategy guarantees safety, and a three-input fuzzy controller maps braking intensity, vehicle speed, and battery state of charge. Chaotic search is introduced into the improved whale optimization algorithm to optimize the fuzzy membership functions. The strategy is validated through Simulink and vehicle dynamics co-simulation under multiple braking intensities and a mining-representative China Typical City Bus Cycle with real mine roadway gradients. The optimized strategy meets braking safety requirements in all conditions. Over the driving cycle, the driving range increases from 80 to 88 km, a 10% improvement over conventional fuzzy control and 29% over the no-recovery baseline. The controller recovers 2384 kJ, 50.2% more than conventional fuzzy control, exceeding the ideal braking force distribution strategy and the Economic Commission for Europe Regulation 13-induced strategy, while remaining competitive with the regenerative energy maximization strategy. This work shows that algorithmic optimization of fuzzy membership functions can substantially improve both energy economy and braking safety in underground mining transport.

title: Constraint-aware PI control of residual chlorine in a drinking water distribution network: Data-driven modeling, robustness analysis, and direct EPANET validation
abstract: Maintaining a disinfectant residual throughout a drinking water distribution network is a dynamic control problem because transport and reaction processes produce location-dependent gains and delays. This study developed a reproducible, constraint-aware workflow linking independently validated node-specific models with proportional-integral (PI) control, with the contribution lying in the systematic integration and validation framework rather than in a new PI architecture. Two independent multilevel EPANET experiments supplied seven days for identification and five days for external validation at 60 s sampling. For each of 22 nodes, 1,080 autoregressive models with exogenous input were screened using identification data only and frozen before external evaluation. PI-SIMC was compared with setpoint-weighted and Smith-predictor variants under saturation, actuation delay, and anti-windup. The primary robustness analysis comprised 13,200 paired Monte Carlo simulations; a further 4,400 matched-tuning runs isolated the effect of the Smith predictor. The 22 models achieved median external fit of 88.18% and RMSE of 0.0541 mg/L. PI-SIMC achieved median IAE of 0.682 mg·h/L, RMSE of 0.060 mg/L, and 85.4% time within ±0.05 mg/L. Setpoint weighting reduced nominal overshoot from 5.89% to 1.43% for a median IAE cost of 1.6%. With identical PI2 tuning, Smith prediction lowered median IAE at 15 of 22 nodes but increased it at seven, confirming a node-dependent effect. title: Sensorimotor Impairments and Task-Specific Virtual Reality-Augmented Balance Rehabilitation in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review.
venue: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
abstract: Balance impairment in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) reflects interacting respiratory, muscular, sensory, cognitive, and behavioral constraints. Virtual reality (VR) and exergaming offer repeated practice and feedback, but technologies and exercise content vary substantially. This narrative review integrates COPD clinical and physiological evidence with indirect motor-learning literature to propose an impairment-oriented, task-specific rehabilitation framework. Study selection was performed by one reviewer, retrieval was selective, and no formal risk-of-bias or certainty assessment was undertaken. Direct VR-specific balance evidence in stable COPD remains sparse. A principal positive balance finding comes from hospitalized patients with acute exacerbation who received additional somatosensory game exercise alongside conventional therapy; it cannot establish effectiveness in stable outpatient or home populations or isolate a VR-specific effect. Pulmonary-rehabilitation outcomes, functional mobility, direct balance outcomes, and feasibility are considered separately. The framework links observed impairments to assessments, candidate tasks, proposed mechanisms, and outcomes, with explicit distinctions between direct COPD-VR evidence, non-VR COPD evidence, indirect evidence, and hypotheses. Current findings do not establish restoration of sensory function, durable sensory reweighting, or fall prevention. Dose-matched trials with mechanism-specific measures, retention, transfer, systematic safety reporting, and patient-relevant outcomes are needed before the proposed matching rules can be validated.

title: External load profiles across game-based training formats, friendly matches, and official matches in elite professional soccer players.
abstract: This study compared the per-minute external load profiles of different game-based training formats with those of friendly and official matches in elite professional soccer players. Eighteen elite male professional soccer players competing in the Turkish Super League (age: 26.3 ± 5.2 years; height: 180.9 ± 5.3 cm; body mass: 77.9 ± 5.2 kg) participated in the study. External load data were collected over a three-week competitive period using 15-Hz global positioning system (GPS) devices. Four game-based training formats (3 vs. 3, 8 vs. 8, 9 vs. 9, and 10 vs. 10), together with two friendly matches and two official league matches, were analyzed. All external load variables were expressed per minute of playing time. Total distance (TD), high-speed running distance (HSR), sprint distance, high acceleration-deceleration distance (Acc + Dec), and high metabolic power (HMP) distance were compared using repeated-measures ANOVA. Significant differences were observed across conditions for all variables (all p < 0.001; partial η² = 0.36-0.73). The 3 vs. 3 condition showed the greatest per-minute TD, high Acc + Dec, and HMP distances, whereas friendly and official matches showed the greatest per-minute HSR and sprint distances. Relative to official match play, each condition showed a distinct per-minute external load profile, exceeding match values for some variables while falling below them for others. These values reflect per-minute (rate-based) external load rather than total accumulated load. These findings indicate that game-based training conditions were associated with distinct per-minute external load profiles, with no single condition matching official match play across all variables. title: Temporal Logic Tensor Networks: Foundations of Temporal Reasoning in Neural Networks
abstract: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and broader intervals. Neither point-wise nor purely interval semantics suffices: the former fragments events into frame-level snapshots lacking overall event identification; the latter treats intervals as atomic truth-values, ignoring state trajectories. We introduce Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (tLTN), a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework addressing this duality via a formal, multi-sorted logic where events and states are structurally interdependent. Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation.
